power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.63", "p=0.13"), Sentence = c("Seventy-one percent of participants were classified as responders for composite symptom burden (median 4.65 to 2.36; p<0.001), while 29% showed no meaningful multisystem improvement (3.59 to 3.58; p=0.63).", "No demographic or clinical variables were strongly associated with predominant responsiveness; however, more frequent injection showed a non-significant trend toward greater responsiveness (OR 2.37, 95% CI 0.79-7.58; p=0.13)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Pernicious Anaemia is an autoimmune-mediated disorder of vitamin B 12 absorption, managed using fixed-interval vitamin B 12 replacement regimens.
Despite treatment, many patients report persistent or recurrent symptoms, suggesting substantial inter-individual variability in treatment response.
More tailored approaches may therefore be needed to reduce symptom burden and improve quality of life.
This prospective observational study used high-frequency longitudinal digital symptom monitoring to characterise symptom dynamics and heterogeneity in treatment response.
UK adults with pernicious anaemia, recruited via the Pernicious Anaemia Society, selfreported daily symptoms (severity 0-10) and vitamin B 12 treatments over three months.
Analyses quantified within-and between-person variability, injection-aligned symptom response kinetics, and differences in treatment response by injection frequency.
Sixty-eight participants were included in the longitudinal analyses, providing >5,100 persondays of symptom data over a mean of 76 days (SD 28).
text.formatted: Sixty-eight participants were included in the longitudinal analyses, providing >5,100 persondays of symptom data over a mean of 76 days (SD 28).

text.text: Most symptom variance was attributable to stable between-person differences (ICC range, 0.58-0.80), indicating the persistence of individual symptom phenotypes.
Vitamin B 12 injections were followed by rapid symptom improvement, although magnitude and timing varied markedly by symptom domain.

Seventy-one percent of participants were classified as responders for composite symptom burden (median 4.65 to 2.36; p<0.001), while 29% showed no meaningful multisystem improvement (3.59 to 3.58; p=0.63).
text.formatted: Seventy-one percent of participants were classified as responders for composite symptom burden (median 4.65 to 2.36; p<0.001), while 29% showed no meaningful multisystem improvement (3.59 to 3.58; p=0.63).

text.text: Cognitive symptoms improved earliest, typically within 24-72 hours; fatigue and pain responses peaked at 3-5 days, and neurosensory symptoms at 4-6 days.
Responses clustered within individuals, indicating distinct responder phenotypes.
Overall symptom burden improved most among participants receiving monthly injections, whereas those injecting weekly or more often had higher preinjection burden and smaller improvements.
These findings suggest that fixed-interval vitamin B 12 replacement may not adequately reflect individual variation in symptom recurrence and treatment response.
High-frequency digital symptom monitoring may provide a practical framework for characterising these patterns and for evaluating more individualised, symptom-guided vitamin B 12 management.
Pernicious Anaemia (PA) is a life-long, autoimmune disease characterised by the destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to impaired vitamin B 12  (B 12 ) absorption [1], [2].

text.text: PA remains an overlooked condition associated with substantial diagnostic delay or misdiagnosis and one-size-fits-all management approaches [3], [4].

text.text: In the United Kingdom, maintenance treatment typically consists of fixed-interval intramuscular hydroxocobalamin injections every two or three months [3], [5].

text.text: However, more than half of patients seek more frequent treatment, either through their GP or often self-administered, to achieve better symptom control [4], [6].

text.text: People with PA report a wide range of neurological, cognitive, mood-related and systemic symptoms, including paraesthesia, balance problems, memory and concentration difficulties, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, depression and anxiety [2], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11].

text.text: Many of these symptoms are non-specific and may also occur in other autoimmune, neurological or nutritional conditions, making attribution to pernicious anaemia challenging.
Importantly, some individuals continue to experience persistent or recurrent symptoms despite long-term vitamin B 12 replacement.
The optimal approach to long-term maintenance treatment remains uncertain.
Fixed-interval regimens are widely used, yet many patients report symptom recurrence before their next scheduled injection and seek more frequent treatment.
It also remains unclear whether persistent symptoms reflect inadequate treatment, irreversible consequences of previous B12 deficiency, co-existing conditions, or other factors.
The James Lind Alliance Priority Setting Partnership identified improving management and treatment as a key research priority in PA [5].

text.text: Addressing this priority requires a better understanding of what symptoms arise in PA, how each symptom varies between and within individuals and importantly if and to what degree these symptoms respond to B 12 treatment.

Daily digital symptom tracking offers a promising approach to capturing within-and betweenindividual variability in PA symptomatology that is not detectable through conventional, cross-sectional designs.

In rheumatoid arthritis, endometriosis, menstrual health and multiple sclerosis, digital symptom monitoring has characterised heterogeneous symptom trajectories, informed clinical decision-making and supported more effective personalised management strategies [12], [13].

text.text: Symptoms in PA are central to daily functioning but can vary markedly in their severity, timing and responsiveness to B12 therapy between individuals.

Existing studies have relied largely on cross-sectional or retrospective assessments, limiting understanding of short-term symptom fluctuations and treatment-aligned response dynamics [3], [7], [10], [14].

text.text: Longitudinal daily monitoring across multiple treatment cycles provides an opportunity to characterise within-person symptom trajectories, identify treatment-response phenotypes, and evaluate whether fixed-interval maintenance regimens adequately reflect the heterogeneity of symptom response observed in clinical practice.
This is consistent with current NICE guidance, which recommends adjusting maintenance treatment according to symptom severity [15].

text.text: In the current study, we aimed to characterise symptom dynamics and treatment response among individuals living with PA using longitudinal daily digital symptom tracking.
This study used an observational, prospective daily symptom-tracking design delivered as an online questionnaire hosted on Qualtrics.
The survey was developed by the University of Surrey research team in collaboration with the PAS to ensure relevance and feasibility for daily completion.
Participants were recruited between April 2023 and May 2023.
Data collection took place between June 2023 and October 2023.
Participants were invited to complete the survey once per day for up to three months, providing repeated measures of B 12 treatment, symptom presentation and severity over time.
All participants provided electronic written informed consent prior to participation via an online consent form integrated within the Qualtrics platform.
The study was conducted remotely, with participants completing surveys on personal devices.
Participants were recruited via the PAS research repository, a database of individuals who had previously expressed interest in participating in research related to PA [4].

text.text: Eligible individuals were invited by email and provided with a participant information sheet, electronic consent form and a link to the baseline Qualtrics survey.
Automated daily reminder emails containing the survey link were sent throughout the participation period to support engagement and minimise missing data.
As this was an exploratory prospective observational study, no formal a priori sample-size calculation was performed.
Recruitment was based on feasibility and the number of eligible participants available through the PAS research repository during the study period.
Participants who withdrew from the study were excluded from the longitudinal analyses.
Prospective daily reporting and automated reminders were used to minimise recall bias and missing observations.
Injection-level observations were aggregated within participants before cohort-level analyses to reduce disproportionate weighting of participants receiving more frequent injections.
Participants were eligible to take part if they met all of the following criteria:

Were aged 18 years or older • Self-reported a diagnosis of PA, and indicated that their diagnosis had been supported by at least one of the following: positive intrinsic factor autoantibodies, a positive Schilling test (historical), or endoscopic/histological evidence of autoimmune gastritis (AIG) • Reported current treatment with intramuscular or subcutaneous B 12 injections.
Participants could also use additional B 12 preparations, including oral tablets, sublingual formulations, sprays, or patches.

• Reported experiencing symptoms attributed to PA; • Were resident in the United Kingdom; • Had access to the internet and a personal device (mobile phone, tablet, or computer) to complete the online survey.
Participants completed a brief daily online questionnaire capturing B 12 treatment exposure, symptom presence and severity, and overall wellbeing (Supplementary Table 1).

text.text: Each day, participants reported whether they had received any B 12 treatment and, if so, specified the route of administration (intramuscular injection, subcutaneous injection, oral, sublingual, spray, or patch) and formulation.
Participants then reported symptom presence and rated severity from a list derived from prior work (Supplementary Note 1).
Symptom severity was recorded using an 11-point numerical rating scale (0-10), where 0 indicated symptom absence and 10 indicated maximal severity.

For each symptom, participants were provided with standardised quality-of-life and functional impairment anchored severity definitions: • Mild symptom: The symptom is noticeable but doesn't interfere with daily living activities, you get used to it and adapt to the symptom.
• Moderate symptom: The symptom is distracting throughout the day but can be ignored for some time when focusing on daily activities.
• Severe symptom: The symptom significantly interferes with daily activities and cannot be ignored at all.
Overall wellbeing was recorded on a 10-point scale from 1 (excellent) to 10 (poor), with lower scores indicating better wellbeing, and was analysed separately from symptom burden.
Within-day items were compulsory, although participants could miss days and resume subsequently.

A baseline questionnaire collected demographic and clinical characteristics, including age, sex, age at PA diagnosis, duration of symptoms before diagnosis, family history of PA, and co-existing autoimmune conditions.
The survey required approximately five minutes to complete.
Participants were invited to complete a post-study feedback survey.
Each participant was assigned a unique identifier to enable longitudinal linkage while preserving anonymity.
Survey data were stored on the Qualtrics platform and exported to Microsoft Excel and R for cleaning and analysis following study completion.
Missing daily entries were retained as missing and not imputed.
All analyses were conducted in R (version 2023.12.0).
Symptom severity scores were treated as ordinal repeated measures and analysed using non-parametric tests.

Analyses Within-person treatment effects were estimated using temporally aligned three-day preinjection (t-3 to t-1) and three-day post-injection (t+1 to t+3) windows, restricted to injections isolated from adjacent doses.
To avoid over-representation of frequent injectors, injectionlevel summaries were aggregated to participant-level mean pre-and post-treatment severities prior to cohort-level analyses.
Paired changes were summarised using medians and interquartile ranges and tested using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
For injection-frequency analyses, participants were grouped according to their predominant injection schedule: 2-3 monthly, monthly, every 2-3 weeks, or weekly or more often.
For comparisons of standard versus non-standard treatment frequency, 2-3 monthly treatment was classified as standard and all more frequent schedules as non-standard.
Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were calculated to partition within-and betweenparticipant variance.
Symptom co-occurrence was assessed using Spearman's rank correlation matrices.

Treatment responder status was classified using pre-specified absolute and percentage change thresholds informed by IMMPACT and minimal clinically important difference (MCID) criteria [16], [17], [18], [19], [20].

text.text: Person-level clustering of response was examined using multilevel logistic regression models with random intercepts for participants and symptoms.

Exploratory analyses examined associations between predominant responder status and age, sex, age at PA diagnosis, duration of symptoms before diagnosis, presence of additional autoimmune conditions, and injection frequency.
Odds ratios were reported with 95% confidence intervals.

Full methodological details are provided in the Supplementary Methods (Supplementary Notes 2-5), including descriptive analyses, injection-cycle construction, individualised response-window modelling, and responder phenotyping with multilevel clustering analyses.
To examine broader patterns of symptom response beyond individual symptoms, related symptoms were grouped into clinically and biologically informed domains.

Three domains were constructed: cognitive (poor concentration, memory loss, nominal aphasia), neurosensory (paraesthesia, nerve pain, dizziness, tinnitus), and pain-fatigue-affective (fatigue, myalgia, irritability).

A further three participants were excluded because 243 of low survey completion (<20%), leaving 68 participants in the longitudinal analyses.

text.text: Distinct symptom-specific response kinetics were observed.
Median symptom scores increased in the days immediately preceding injection and declined sharply thereafter, consistent with injections being administered during periods of rising symptom burden.

Cognitive symptoms (poor concentration, memory loss and nominal aphasia) demonstrated rapid early improvement, with median severity falling sharply between Day 0 and Day 1 and reaching a plateau by Days 2-3 before gradual recurrence.

In contrast, fatigue and myalgia showed more gradual and sustained improvement, with fatigue reaching its lowest median severity around Day 6 and remaining below pre-treatment levels throughout the observation period.
Several symptoms displayed oscillatory ("yo-yo") patterns across Days 1-7, indicating modal rather than linear recovery trajectories.
In general, neuro-sensory symptoms (paraesthesia, nerve pain, tinnitus, dizziness) showed greater heterogeneity and more delayed response kinetics.
Paraesthesia and nerve pain exhibited progressive reductions peaking around Days 2-3, while dizziness demonstrated rapid early improvement with near-complete median resolution by Days 3-4.

Composite symptom burden and the cognitive and neuro-sensory domain scores closely mirrored the dominant trajectories of their component symptoms, showing sharp early reductions followed by stabilisation.

Visualisation of individual injection trajectories further highlighted marked inter-individual variability in baseline symptom scores and substantial heterogeneity in the magnitude and durability of the post-injection response (Fig 3b & Supplementary Fig 2).

This study provides the first longitudinal characterisation of symptom dynamics and treatment response among individuals living with PA using daily symptomatology tracking.

Despite all participants receiving long-term maintenance B 12 therapy, many continued to experience substantial symptom burden with cyclical worsening before injections and rapid improvement following treatment.
Across the cohort, symptom severity varied markedly between individuals but was relatively stable within individuals over time, indicating persistent inter-individual symptomatology.

In general, B 12 injections produced rapid and clinically meaningful symptom improvements across multiple domains, although the magnitude, timing, and durability of response varied substantially both between symptoms and between individuals.
Notably, treatment responses clustered strongly within individuals across symptom systems, revealing a latent responder/non-responder phenotype that transcends individual symptom categories.
The present study is consistent with prior literature showing that PA has a broad and heterogeneous symptom profile spanning cognitive, neurological and systemic domains [3], [7], [10], [14], [22].

text.text: It extends the literature by quantifying within-person symptom dynamics and injection-aligned response kinetics.

One prior study has quantitatively examined patientreported symptom response to B 12 treatment at scale. Kornic et al. (2016) conducted a retrospective survey assessing historical treatment regimen, demonstrating that injection therapy and more frequent dosing were associated with greater symptom improvement than oral therapy and long-interval maintenance schedules [23].

text.text: While conceptually in line with our findings, their analyses were based on long-term recall and treatment averages and could not characterise temporal kinetics or individual response phenotypes.
The findings also support previous suggestions that symptom improvement may begin within days but can evolve over weeks to months, particularly for neurological symptoms [9], [15], [24], [25].

text.text: However, the timing and duration of improvement have not previously been quantified at high temporal resolution or at the level of individual symptoms and injection events.
Daily symptom tracking demonstrated that symptom burden in PA is characterised stable person-specific symptoms across cognitive, neurological and systemic domains.
Neurosensory symptoms such as paraesthesia and dizziness exhibited the highest betweenperson stability, whereas cognitive symptoms showed greater within-person fluctuation.
These patterns may reflect differences in the mechanisms underlying symptom persistence and responsiveness.
Correlations among cognitive symptoms further demonstrated symptom clustering, suggesting that some symptoms vary together rather than independently.
Treatment response also clustered strongly within participants across symptoms and symptom domains, indicating that individuals with PA are not likely to follow a uniform therapeutic response.
Instead, participants exhibit distinct treatment-response phenotypes with varying kinetic profiles and treatment sensitivities.
These findings suggest that fixedinterval replacement schedules may not capture the range of treatment responses observed in practice.
While observational and not causal, the divergence in symptom trajectories across individuals supports further evaluation of more flexible and pragmatic dosing strategies.
A central finding of this study is that response to B 12 injections is not only heterogeneous in magnitude but also in temporal kinetics, revealing distinct response kinetics across participants.
Across symptoms, improvement did not occur uniformly in the immediate postinjection period.

Cognitive symptoms exhibit rapid responses, typically peaking within 24-72 hours, whereas fatigue and pain-related symptoms showed more gradual but sustained improvement, and neuro-sensory symptoms exhibited delayed, heterogeneous, and often oscillatory ("yo-yo") response trajectories.

Importantly, treatment responses clustered within individuals across symptoms and domains, with participants often showing broadly concordant improvement or minimal change across multiple symptom groups.

However, as symptom severity was self-reported, this pattern could also partly reflect consistent reporting behaviour or expectancy effects, whereby individuals' beliefs about treatment effectiveness influence symptom ratings across domains.
Given the observational design, our findings cannot distinguish biological treatment sensitivity from reporting-related effects.
Rather, they indicate stable individual-level response patterns that warrant further investigation under controlled conditions.
Injection frequency did not exert a uniform effect on symptom burden across the cohort.
Importantly, these findings were observed among individuals receiving long-term maintenance B 12 therapy, who would generally be expected to have stable symptom control.
Instead, many participants continued to experience recurrent symptom exacerbations between injections, suggesting that maintenance treatment did not consistently provide sustained symptom control.

Distinct symptom-and domain-specific dose-response patterns were observed, indicating that optimal injection frequency may vary by symptom system rather than following a simple "more is better" paradigm.

Notably, the highest injection frequencies were not associated with greater multisystem symptom control; composite symptom burden showed its largest improvement under monthly regimens, whereas weekly-or-more-frequent dosing was associated with comparatively little improvement.

However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, as reported injection frequency may reflect attempts to improve symptom control rather than objectively an individual's optimal treatment regimen.
Frequent injection use may reflect two distinct clinical scenarios.
In some individuals, rapid symptom recurrence despite preserved responsiveness may indicate undertreatment under standard maintenance schedules.

In others, escalating injection frequency may represent a compensatory response to reduced responsiveness to B 12 treatment, whereby increasing injection frequency provides limited symptomatic benefit.

The relatively modest treatment effects observed in this group, together with strong within-person clustering of treatment response across symptom domains, suggest that persistent symptoms may not be explained solely by insufficient dosing.

Alternative explanations include reduced biological responsiveness to B 12 treatment, irreversible neurological sequelae following delayed diagnosis, or symptom recurrence after transition from more frequent to standard maintenance regimens [26], [27], [28].

text.text: This may help explain why increasing injection frequency does not uniformly restore symptom control in all participants.
Collectively, these findings support a more individualised, symptom-guided approach to maintenance treatment rather than a single fixed dosing schedule.

Finally, almost half of participants reported receiving B 12 injections more frequently than the current standard 2-3-month maintenance regimen, and many also used additional over-thecounter B12 preparations e.g. oral, sublingual between injections.
Although adjunctive therapies were not formally evaluated, their widespread use may reflect unmet symptom control needs within current maintenance schedules.

This may suggest that some individuals do not achieve satisfactory symptom relief with any fixed-interval replacement alone [15], [21], [29], although it may also suggest adherence to a more is better approach.

text.text: This study represents the first high-resolution longitudinal characterisation of symptom dynamics and treatment response in PA using daily digital patient-reported outcome measures.

Rich within-person sampling and injection-aligned modelling enabled evaluation of symptom trajectories and treatment response beyond what is possible using crosssectional or recall-based study designs.

Participants demonstrated high engagement with daily symptom tracking, with an overall completion rate of 84% and a mean of 76 days of data contributed per participant (SD 28). direct comparison with other remote monitoring studies is limited by inconsistent reporting of adherence [30], this supports the feasibility and scalability of longitudinal digital symptom tracking in PA.

text.text: Several limitations should be acknowledged.

Recruitment through a patient organisation may have preferentially included individuals with greater symptom burden or engagement with their condition, potentially limiting generalisability to the wider PA population.
Symptom severity and treatment exposure were self-reported, introducing potential reporting bias and misclassification.

Although daily prospective reporting substantially reduces recall bias compared with retrospective surveys, symptom ratings remain subjective and may be influenced by symptom awareness or expectations of treatment response [31].

text.text: Although high-frequency sampling improves temporal resolution, individual response kinetics may extend beyond the post-injection windows captured in this study.
Consequently, a subset of participants classified as non-responders may include delayed or atypical responders whose symptom improvements fall outside the analysed response periods.
In addition, co-existing nutritional deficiencies (e.g. iron and/or folate deficiency) were not evaluated and may also have contributed to symptom burden.
Although the within-person analytic design mitigates many time-invariant confounders, residual confounding from non-PA-related symptom drivers cannot be excluded.
This work establishes a foundation for precision-guided management of PA and highlights several priorities for future research.
First, mechanistic studies are needed to define the biological determinants underlying stable responder phenotypes and symptom-specific treatment kinetics.
Understanding the drivers of differential responsiveness will be essential for explaining refractory symptom patterns and informing targeted therapeutic strategies.

Second, intervention studies comparing fixed-interval dosing with personalised injection schedules tailored to individual symptom trajectories are warranted to establish evidencebased maintenance models for PA.

Although the present study cannot determine causality or optimal dosing strategies, the observed heterogeneity in treatment response provides a strong rationale for pragmatic trials evaluating symptom-guided maintenance approaches.
PA is a heterogeneous multisystem condition with marked variability in symptom burden and treatment responsiveness despite maintenance B 12 therapy.
B 12 injections produced rapid symptom improvement, but response kinetics varied substantially between and within individuals and symptom domains.
These findings support evaluation of more individualised, symptom-guided maintenance strategies.

Specifically, we sought to: (1) characterise symptomatology presentation and burden across multiple B 12 treatment cycles; (2) quantify within-and between-individual variability in symptom severity; (3) identify treatment-response phenotypes; and (4) evaluate the impact of standard versus non-standard treatment frequencies on symptom trajectories.
We identified substantial between-person variation in symptom burden, alongside distinct injection-aligned patterns and individual differences in treatment response.

Third, integration of longitudinal digital symptom monitoring into clinical care requires formal evaluation.
Digital platforms enabling real-time symptom tracking, trajectory visualisation and clinician-linked data sharing may support more individualised treatment adjustment.
Such approaches may also complement conventional biomarker monitoring by providing additional information on day-to-day symptom burden and treatment response.

Preliminary pilot work using wearable smartwatch technology (unpublished data) has demonstrated the feasibility of continuous physiological monitoring in PA, supporting future integration of objective digital measures alongside symptom-based tracking within precision treatment models.
